uncited: This family accelerates the back-projection step of tomographic reconstruction by mapping projection weights to volume expansion coefficients on parallel hardware [Back-projection](2450-back-projection.md).

It distinguishes itself from CPU-based siblings by leveraging GPU compute units (OpenCL) to perform the $O(V \cdot P)$ accumulation of voxel contributions, utilizing either global memory buffers or hardware texture caches for data access [Back-projection](2450-back-projection.md).
All methods in this family solve the inverse problem of reconstructing a 3D volume $V$ from $P$ 2D projections.
The core mechanism is the parallel execution of the back-projection kernel, where each work-item (thread) corresponds to a unique voxel in the output volume.
For a voxel at physical coordinates $(x, y, z)$ and a projection angle $\theta_p$, the ray is traced back to the detector plane.
The detector coordinates $(u, v)$ are computed using the Source-to-Object Distance ($sod$) and Source-to-Detector Distance ($sdd$).

Note: Some implementations use simplified linear approximations or different axis conventions (e.g., [4991-gpu-backprojection-with-global-memory-buffer.md](4991-gpu-backprojection-with-global-memory-buffer.md) uses $u = x_{rot} \cdot \frac{sdd}{sod}$).
The value from the projection image at $(u, v)$ is accumulated into the voxel.

A weighting factor $\frac{sod^2}{U^2}$ is often applied to account for cone-beam divergence, where $U$ is the distance from the source to the voxel plane along the ray [5111-gpu-backprojection-using-opencl-image-textures.md](5111-gpu-backprojection-using-opencl-image-textures.md).
After all $P$ projections are processed, the volume is scaled by $\frac{\pi}{P}$ [4991-gpu-backprojection-with-global-memory-buffer.md](4991-gpu-backprojection-with-global-memory-buffer.md).

Projections are typically stored in column-major order (`u * H + v`) in host memory but may be transposed to row-major (`v * W + u`) for GPU coalescing or image texture compatibility [5110-gpu-backprojection-using-opencl-buffers.md](5110-gpu-backprojection-using-opencl-buffers.md).
Originating from the need to accelerate Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) and parallel-beam reconstruction algorithms, GPU-based back-projection became standard with the advent of OpenCL and CUDA.
The specific implementations cited rely on OpenCL for cross-vendor compatibility.

The use of image textures for interpolation exploits dedicated GPU hardware units, reducing arithmetic intensity [5111-gpu-backprojection-using-opencl-image-textures.md](5111-gpu-backprojection-using-opencl-image-textures.md).
